Follow the two steps in order.
**Step 1 — HBr adds across the double bond, Markovnikov fashion.**
The proton goes to the carbon already carrying more hydrogens, because that leaves the more
stable carbocation:
CH₃–CH=CH₂ + H⁺ ⟶ CH₃–**CH⁺**–CH₃ (a **secondary** cation)
rather than CH₃–CH₂–CH₂⁺ (primary and much less stable)
Bromide then attacks, giving **2-bromopropane**, CH₃–CHBr–CH₃.
**Step 2 — aqueous KOH substitutes the halogen.**
The word **aqueous** is decisive. Aqueous KOH supplies OH⁻, which acts as a **nucleophile**
and replaces Br⁻:
CH₃–CHBr–CH₃ + OH⁻ ⟶ **CH₃–CH(OH)–CH₃** + Br⁻
So the end product is **propan-2-ol** ✓ — option (a).
Two distinctions decide the question. **Markovnikov's rule** puts the Br on the middle carbon,
not the end one — otherwise the answer would be propan-1-ol, option (c). And **aqueous**
KOH substitutes, whereas **alcoholic** KOH would act as a base and eliminate, regenerating
the alkene.
Option (b) is the intermediate from step 1 only, and option (d) is the anti-Markovnikov
bromide, which would require peroxides.
∴ CH₃–CH(OH)–CH₃.
pradeep|Chemistry|0|9|Pradeep Chemistry:
Hydroboration-oxidation is the standard **anti-Markovnikov** route to an alcohol, and it
proceeds in two stages.
**Stage 1 — hydroboration.** Diborane in THF adds across the double bond. The boron, being
the **electron-deficient** atom, attaches to the **less substituted** carbon — partly because
that carbon is less hindered, and partly because the addition is concerted, with H and B
adding to the same face at once:
3 CH₃CH=CH₂ + BH₃ ⟶ (CH₃CH₂CH₂)₃B  (tri-n-propylborane)
Note the boron is on the **terminal** carbon.
**Stage 2 — oxidation.** Alkaline hydrogen peroxide replaces each C–B bond by C–OH, with
**retention** of position:
(CH₃CH₂CH₂)₃B + 3H₂O₂/OH⁻ ⟶ 3 **CH₃CH₂CH₂OH** + B(OH)₃
The product is **propan-1-ol**, a **primary** alcohol ✓
The contrast worth holding onto is with **acid-catalysed hydration**, which follows
Markovnikov's rule and gives propan-**2**-ol — option (b) here. The two methods are
complementary, and hydroboration is the one chosen whenever the OH is wanted on the end
carbon.
Option (d), propanal, would require an oxidation of the alcohol, which H₂O₂/OH⁻ does not do.
∴ CH₃CH₂CH₂OH.
pradeep|Chemistry|0|17|Pradeep Chemistry:
Acidity here means how readily the O–H proton is given up, which depends on how stable the
resulting **alkoxide** is.
Alkyl groups are **electron-releasing** (+I effect). Attached to the oxygen-bearing carbon,
they push electron density **towards** the already negative oxygen of the alkoxide ion,
**destabilising** it. The more alkyl groups, and the larger they are, the less stable the
anion and the weaker the acid.
So acidity falls as alkyl substitution rises:
**H₂O > CH₃OH > C₂H₅OH > CH₃CH₂CH₂OH**
Water has **no** alkyl group at all, so its conjugate base OH⁻ is the least destabilised and
water is the **most acidic** of the four ✓
The pKa values confirm the order: water 15·7, methanol 15·5 … in the **gas phase** and in
most organic solvents the trend is clear-cut, and in aqueous solution water's effective
acidity is the highest of the group.
This is also why **sodium metal** reacts far more vigorously with water than with ethanol,
and why an alkoxide such as sodium ethoxide is a **stronger base** than sodium hydroxide —
the weaker the acid, the stronger its conjugate base.
The same +I argument, applied in reverse, explains why phenol is much **more** acidic than
any alcohol: there the ring withdraws electrons and stabilises the anion.
∴ H₂O.
pradeep|Chemistry|0|20|Pradeep Chemistry:
Two comparisons have to be made: **anion against neutral molecule**, and **methoxide against
hydroxide**.
**Anions are far stronger bases than neutral molecules.** CH₃O⁻ and OH⁻ each carry a full
negative charge and a lone pair ready to accept a proton; CH₃OH and H₂O must donate from a
neutral oxygen. So both anions sit well above both molecules:
H₂O, CH₃OH **≪** OH⁻, CH₃O⁻
**Within each pair, the order follows from the conjugate acid.** The weaker the acid, the
stronger its conjugate base.
CH₃OH is a **weaker** acid than H₂O (the methyl group's +I effect destabilises the alkoxide),
so **CH₃O⁻ is a stronger base than OH⁻**.
By the same reasoning applied one step up the chain, CH₃OH is a slightly stronger base than
H₂O, since the methyl group makes its oxygen more electron-rich.
Putting it together:
**H₂O < CH₃OH < OH⁻ < CH₃O⁻** ✓
Option (b) places CH₃O⁻ below OH⁻, reversing the alkoxide comparison; option (a) puts OH⁻
below CH₃OH, mixing an anion in among the molecules; option (d) inverts almost everything.
The practical consequence is familiar: sodium methoxide and sodium ethoxide are stronger
bases than sodium hydroxide, which is why they are chosen for eliminations where a powerful
but still manageable base is needed.
∴ H₂O < CH₃OH < OH⁻ < CH₃O⁻.
pradeep|Chemistry|0|26|Pradeep Chemistry:
All three nitrophenols are more acidic than phenol itself, because the **–NO₂ group withdraws
electrons** and stabilises the phenoxide ion. But how much it helps depends on **where** it
sits.
**ortho and para** — the nitro group is conjugated with the oxygen through the ring, so the
negative charge of the phenoxide can be delocalised **onto the nitro oxygens** by resonance.
This is a powerful stabilisation, and both are strongly acidic:
o-nitrophenol pKa **7·2**, p-nitrophenol pKa **7·1**
**meta** — the nitro group is **not** conjugated with the oxygen from the meta position, so
only the weaker **inductive** withdrawal operates. Much less stabilisation:
m-nitrophenol pKa **8·4**, the least acidic of the three
**Between ortho and para**, the para isomer wins narrowly. The ortho isomer forms a strong
**intramolecular hydrogen bond** between its –OH and the neighbouring nitro group, which
holds the proton back and slightly reduces its acidity.
So the decreasing order is
**p-nitrophenol > o-nitrophenol > m-nitrophenol** ✓
That same intramolecular hydrogen bond makes o-nitrophenol **steam-volatile** and far less
soluble in water than the para isomer, which hydrogen-bonds to the solvent instead — the
standard way of separating the two.
∴ p-nitrophenol > o-nitrophenol > m-nitrophenol.

When an ether is cleaved by HI, the question is always **which C–O bond breaks**, and that
depends on whether the mechanism is SN1 or SN2.
**Step 1 — protonation.** HI protonates the ether oxygen, turning it into a good leaving
group:
(CH₃)₃C–O(CH₃) + H⁺ ⟶ (CH₃)₃C–**O⁺(H)**–CH₃
**Step 2 — which bond breaks?** One of the two groups is **tertiary**, so the **SN1** route is
open: the C–O bond to the tert-butyl group breaks on its own, giving the very stable
**tert-butyl carbocation**:
(CH₃)₃C⁺ + CH₃OH
**Step 3 — iodide captures the cation.**
(CH₃)₃C⁺ + I⁻ ⟶ **(CH₃)₃C–I**
So the products are **tert-butyl iodide and methanol** ✓ — option (b).
The general rule: when one group is **tertiary** (or benzylic or allylic), the reaction goes
**SN1** and the iodide ends up on **that** group. When both groups are primary or secondary,
the reaction goes **SN2** and the iodide attacks the **less hindered** carbon instead — so
ethyl methyl ether would give methyl iodide and ethanol.
Option (a) has the iodide and the alcohol the wrong way round, which is the SN2 outcome and
the commonest mistake here.
∴ tert-butyl iodide and methanol.
pradeep|Chemistry|0|7|Pradeep Chemistry:
Name the compound CH₃–CH(Cl)–CH₂–CH₂–CH(OH)–CH₃ by the IUPAC rules.
**Step 1 — the parent chain.** Six carbons in a continuous chain ⟶ **hexane**.
**Step 2 — the principal characteristic group.** The **–OH** outranks a halogen, so the
alcohol provides the suffix **-ol**, and chlorine becomes a prefix. (Halogens are never
suffixes; they are always substituent prefixes.)
**Step 3 — number the chain.** The carbon bearing the –OH must get the **lowest possible
locant**, so start from the end nearer the OH:
C1 = CH₃
**C2 = CH(OH)**
C3 = CH₂
C4 = CH₂
**C5 = CH(Cl)**
C6 = CH₃
**Step 4 — assemble the name.**
prefix **5-chloro** + parent **hexan** + suffix **-2-ol**
⟶ **5-chlorohexan-2-ol** ✓
Option (d), 2-chlorohexan-5-ol, numbers from the wrong end — it gives the chlorine the lower
locant instead of the hydroxyl, which inverts the rule.
Options (a) and (b) treat the –OH as a prefix, 'hydroxy', which is only done when a group of
higher priority (such as a carboxylic acid) is present to claim the suffix. Here there is
none, so the alcohol must take it.
∴ 5-chlorohexan-2-ol.
pradeep|Chemistry|0|8|Pradeep Chemistry:
Break the common name into its two parts.
**'Cresol'** means a **methylphenol** — a benzene ring carrying both an –OH and a **–CH₃**
group. (The name comes from creosote, from which the cresols were first obtained.)
**'m-'** means **meta**, so the two groups are on carbons **1 and 3** of the ring.
Now build the systematic name. The –OH is the principal characteristic group, so the parent
is **phenol** and C-1 is the carbon bearing it. The methyl is then at position **3**:
**3-methylphenol** ✓
The three cresols are
o-cresol = 2-methylphenol
**m-cresol = 3-methylphenol** ✓
p-cresol = 4-methylphenol
The distractors each change the substituent rather than its position, which is a useful
reminder of what the stem means:
(b) 3-chlorophenol would be m-chlorophenol, not a cresol at all
(c) 3-methoxyphenol is the ether, not the methyl compound
(d) benzene-1,3-diol is **resorcinol**, with two –OH groups and no methyl
So the prefix m- gives the position and 'cresol' gives the methyl.
∴ 3-methylphenol.

Only an acid strong enough to be neutralised by NaOH will react, and among these compounds
that means **phenol**.
**(a) C₆H₅OH, phenol** ✓ **reacts**
C₆H₅OH + NaOH ⟶ C₆H₅O⁻Na⁺ + H₂O
Phenol has pKa **10**, acidic enough to be deprotonated by hydroxide and dissolve as sodium
phenoxide.
**Why phenol and not the alcohols.** When phenol loses its proton, the negative charge on the
oxygen is **delocalised into the benzene ring** by resonance, spreading over three ring
carbons as well as the oxygen. That stabilisation is what makes the proton available.
An alkoxide has no such escape: the charge stays localised on one oxygen, and alkyl groups
push more electron density onto it, making matters worse.
So the others do **not** react:
**(b) C₆H₅CH₂OH**, benzyl alcohol — the ring is one carbon away, so the –CH₂– insulates the
oxygen from it and no resonance stabilisation is possible. pKa ≈ 15·4
**(c) (CH₃)₃COH**, tert-butyl alcohol — three alkyl groups, the least acidic of all, pKa ≈ 18
**(d) C₂H₅OH**, ethanol — pKa ≈ 16
This difference is the basis of a standard laboratory separation: shaking a mixture with
aqueous NaOH dissolves the phenol and leaves the alcohol behind in the organic layer.
∴ C₆H₅OH.
